rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Referent resolution under a sequential deck read.

Closest candidates: chunk3 L39 'right here'/'this worktree' — resolves same-sentence ('this worktree holds the full codebase') plus chunk0 L5 'the side quest window (*m3-quality*)', session-artifact carve-out; chunk7 L71 'came over at the fork' — no prior use of 'the fork' in this file, but the same sentence supplies the contrast that resolves it ('...and may have drifted from the one in your main repo'), i.e. self-resolving within the sentence, not a dangling forward/never-named pointer. No callback into another file's content by position anywhere in body. Every other chunk carries 2+ bullets or a paragraph with its own claim.

Checked all 7 body headers against their chunk content: each names what the chunk delivers ('Phase 1: Author the skill through conversation' → conversational-authoring bullets; 'Phase 3: Ship the skill personal-first' (L54) → content confirms shipping already happened, L58). Closest edge case: chunk7 'What this sets up' (L69) vs. content that is really a housekeeping note about leftover worktree state (L71) — read as a fair summary since the content IS what remains/what-happens-next as a consequence of the exercise's two-window shape (keep/carry/delete decision), not contradicted by it.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Heading grammar is the mood switch, and it is load-bearing.
rules_evaluated.evidence: All 7 body `##` headers are imperative or Phase-labels ('Phase 1/2/3: …', 'Answer from how your codebase really tests', 'Sharpen the skill from what came back', 'Decide if it graduates to the team') except chunk7's 'What this sets up' (L69), which matches the rule's explicit non-violation category 'orientation headers' — it frames a forward-looking wrap-up rather than posing as a law-claim, so it does not owe declarative-claim grammar. Classified non-blocking here (polish/genre-consistency, not comprehension-breaking) — this rule postdates the template's 1/2/3/4/8/10/12-vs-5/6/9/11/13/14 partition and isn't named in either list; applying the template's own stated principle ('I cannot follow this' vs 'this could be tighter'), a mood mismatch on a heading is the latter.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: A bullet earns its slot or dies — three classes that read as rigour and carry nothing.
rules_evaluated.evidence: Checked every surviving bullet against the three classes. The file's own maintainer block (L75, dated 2026-08-25, 'Lean pass... free hands') already names and removes this exact shape: doctrine restatement ('The skill proves itself only when it runs on real code.' — restated the theatre line), self-referential design commentary ('The authoring muscle is what Module 3 installs.' — tagged '§16b' by the note itself), and aphorism kickers ('That's the ship.'; 'Not every skill graduates to a shared kit.'). Closest surviving candidates: chunk1 L21 ('Skills aren't hand-crafted; they're authored through conversation...') restates chunk0 L7's 'What you do' widget line but adds new procedural detail (who does what: student describes, agent drafts) — earns its slot, not pure recitation; chunk4 L52's second sentence ('A skill that names its own gap is more useful to a teammate than one that pretends it's finished.') justifies the decide-or-ship-with-TODO choice just given rather than restating the header or 'The point' line. Neither matches class (a)/(b)/(c) as this rule defines them. Classified non-blocking here for the same reason as rule 15 (postdates the template's explicit partition; a low-value bullet is a tightness/polish concern, not a comprehension failure).
